title: 10  Capability and Requirement Entities
text:
10.2 Capabilities vs. Components: Practical Distinction

10.2.1 When to Use Capabilities
Capabilities describe what a system does. They are:

Stable across implementations: Different technical approaches can provide the same capability
User-facing: Capabilities correspond to features users can observe and use
High-level: Capabilities don’t specify how functionality is implemented

Example: “Process Payments” is a capability. It doesn’t specify whether payments are processed through a REST API, GraphQL, or event-driven architecture.


10.2.2 When to Use Components
Components describe how functionality is implemented. They are:

Technical structures: Components correspond to code modules, services, or deployable units
Implementation-specific: Different implementations may use different component structures
Low-level: Components specify the technical mechanisms for delivering capabilities

Example: “Payment Service” is a component. It specifies a service that handles payment processing through specific interfaces and implementation patterns.


10.2.3 Mapping Capabilities to Components
A single capability may be realized by multiple components working together:
Capability: Process Payments

Realized by components:
  - Payment Gateway (receives payment requests)
  - Payment Processor (processes transactions)
  - Transaction Store (persists transaction records)
  - Fraud Detection Service (validates transactions)
  - Notification Service (sends payment confirmations)
A single component may contribute to multiple capabilities:
Component: Order Service

Contributes to capabilities:
  - Create Order (primary responsibility)
  - Update Inventory (coordinates with inventory)
  - Generate Confirmation (triggers notifications)
  - Track Order Status (provides status updates)

title: 10  Capability and Requirement Entities
text:
10.3 Constraints in Practice

10.3.1 Example Constraints by Type
Performance Constraints:
API Response Time:
  - Metric: p95_latency_ms
  - Threshold: ≤300
  - Scope: int.api.public
  
Throughput:
  - Metric: requests_per_second
  - Threshold: ≥1000
  - Scope: sys.main
Reliability Constraints:
Service Availability:
  - Metric: availability_percentage
  - Threshold: ≥99.9%
  - Scope: comp.api_service
  
Data Durability:
  - Metric: data_loss_probability
  - Threshold: <0.0001%
  - Scope: comp.database
Security Constraints:
Encryption at Rest:
  - Metric: encryption_algorithm
  - Threshold: AES-256
  - Scope: data.user_records
  
Authentication:
  - Metric: authentication_method
  - Threshold: MFA required
  - Scope: int.admin_console
Capacity Constraints:
Concurrent Users:
  - Metric: max_concurrent_users
  - Threshold: 10000
  - Scope: sys.main
  
Storage Capacity:
  - Metric: max_storage_gb
  - Threshold: 10000
  - Scope: comp.database


10.3.2 Constraint Conflicts and Trade-offs
Example 1: Performance vs. Security
System: E-commerce Platform

Constraints:
  - Performance: API response time ≤200ms
  - Security: All requests must undergo comprehensive security checks

Conflict: Comprehensive security checks add latency, potentially violating the performance constraint.

Trade-off decision:
  - Accept slightly higher latency (≤300ms) to maintain security requirements
  - Implement security checks efficiently (caching, parallel validation)
  - Document the trade-off in constraint metadata
Example 2: Availability vs. Cost
System: Data Storage Service

Constraints:
  - Availability: ≥99.99%
  - Cost: Monthly operational cost ≤$10,000

Conflict: Achieving 99.99% availability requires multi-region deployment, exceeding cost constraints.

Trade-off decision:
  - Accept lower availability (99.95%) to meet cost constraints
  - Implement disaster recovery procedures for critical data
  - Prioritize availability for high-value customers
Example 3: Consistency vs. Latency
System: Distributed Database

Constraints:
  - Consistency: Strong consistency required for financial transactions
  - Latency: Read latency ≤50ms

Conflict: Strong consistency requires synchronous replication, increasing read latency.

Trade-off decision:
  - Use strong consistency only for financial operations
  - Use eventual consistency for analytics queries
  - Implement different consistency levels per operation type

title: 11  Components: The Structural Building Blocks
text:
11.0.1 Component vs Module vs Service
Within system architecture, components represent the primary structural units from which systems are constructed. While capabilities describe what a system can do, components represent how those abilities are realized through concrete structural elements.
A component encapsulates a set of responsibilities and exposes defined interfaces through which other components interact with it. Components therefore form the nodes of the architectural structure, connected through interfaces, data flows, and workflows.
In the ontology, components serve as the central elements of the structural layer. Most architectural relations—dependencies, data access, invocation, and orchestration—are defined between components.
In practice, terms such as component, module, and service are often used interchangeably. For architectural representation, however, these concepts must be distinguished.
A component is the general structural unit of the ontology. It represents a bounded element of a system that performs a defined responsibility and interacts with other components through interfaces.
A module refers to a logical grouping of implementation elements within a codebase. Modules are often defined by programming language constructs such as packages, namespaces, or libraries. Modules are therefore primarily organizational structures inside source code.
A service is a component that exposes functionality through a network-accessible interface and operates as an independently deployable runtime unit.
In this sense:
Within the ontology, the component is the canonical entity. Modules and services can be interpreted as specialized forms or projections of components depending on the architectural view being generated.

section: 11.1 Component Type Examples by System Type
text:
11.1 Component Type Examples by System Type

11.1.1 CLI Tool Components
CLI Tool: Text Analyzer
├── CLI Interface (ui)

    - Writes output files

Web Application: E-commerce Platform
├── Web UI (ui)
│   - Provides user interface
│   - Manages client-side state
├── API Service (api_service)
│   - Implements business logic
│   - Handles HTTP requests

│   - Manages transactions
├── Cache (cache)
│   - Stores frequently accessed data

    - Enables asynchronous email sending

API Service: Authentication Service

│   - Enforces rate limiting

│   - Stores active sessions
│   - Enables fast token validation

    - Records authentication events
    - Supports security auditing


11.1.4 Data Pipeline Components
Data Pipeline: Analytics Platform
├── Ingestion Worker (worker)
│   - Consumes raw data from sources
│   - Validates data format
├── Transformation Engine (engine)
│   - Cleans and transforms data
│   - Applies business rules
├── Data Warehouse (storage)
│   - Stores processed data
│   - Supports complex queries
├── Message Broker (broker)
│   - Coordinates data flow between stages
│   - Enables stream processing

    - Triggers batch jobs
    - Manages job dependencies

Agent System: Task Execution System
├── Agent Controller (engine)
│   - Coordinates agent reasoning cycles
│   - Manages tool selection
├── LLM Engine (model)
│   - Generates reasoning steps
│   - Makes tool invocation decisions
├── Tool Executor (worker)
│   - Executes tool calls
│   - Returns tool results
└── Memory Store (storage)
    - Maintains conversation context
    - Stores intermediate results


11.1.6 Component Attributes
Each component in the ontology is described through a set of attributes that capture its architectural role.
Responsibility
The responsibility defines the primary function of the component. It describes what role the component plays within the system architecture.
Inputs and Outputs
Components consume inputs and produce outputs. These inputs and outputs may correspond to:

API requests
events or messages
data streams
command invocations

Explicitly describing inputs and outputs clarifies how components interact with one another.
Dependencies
Components rarely operate independently. Dependencies describe which other components a given component relies upon in order to perform its responsibilities.
Dependency relations may represent synchronous invocation, asynchronous messaging, or data access relationships.
State
Some components maintain internal state, while others operate statelessly. The state attribute describes whether the component stores persistent or transient information during operation.
State characteristics influence system properties such as scalability, fault tolerance, and recovery behavior.
Together, these attributes define the architectural identity of a component.


11.1.7 Component Boundaries
One of the most important architectural decisions concerns where component boundaries should be drawn.
Component boundaries determine responsibility allocation, coupling relationships, and system maintainability. Poorly chosen boundaries can lead to tightly coupled systems that are difficult to evolve.
Two opposing risks must be managed.
If components are too large, responsibilities become entangled and the component becomes difficult to maintain or reuse.
If components are too small, the architecture becomes fragmented and coordination overhead increases.
Several principles help guide boundary decisions.
A component should encapsulate a coherent responsibility. All internal logic should contribute to a single architectural purpose.
Components should expose interaction only through explicit interfaces. Internal details should remain hidden from other parts of the system.
Dependencies between components should remain minimized and directional. Excessive cross-dependencies indicate that boundaries may be incorrectly defined.
Finally, component boundaries should align with operational realities, such as deployment units, scaling boundaries, or ownership responsibilities.
Determining component boundaries is therefore both a structural and operational decision. The ontology provides the conceptual framework for representing these boundaries, while architectural judgment determines how they are applied in specific systems.

title: 11  Components: The Structural Building Blocks
text:
11.2 Component Boundary Decision Framework

11.2.1 Boundary Indicators
Strong indicators that separate components:

Different scaling requirements: One component needs horizontal scaling while another scales vertically
Different failure domains: Failure of one component shouldn’t cascade to others
Different deployment cycles: Components need to be deployed independently
Different ownership: Different teams are responsible for different functionality
Different technology stacks: Components use different programming languages or frameworks
Different data ownership: Components manage separate data domains with different access patterns

Weak indicators (should not alone justify separation):

Code size: Large codebases don’t necessarily require multiple components
Complexity alone: Internal complexity doesn’t always justify component separation
Temporary optimization: Short-term performance needs shouldn’t dictate architecture



11.2.2 Component Boundary Patterns
Domain-Driven Components
Align components with business domains or bounded contexts:
E-commerce System:
  - Order Management (orders, order items, order history)
  - Inventory Management (products, stock levels, suppliers)
  - Customer Management (users, profiles, preferences)
  - Payment Processing (transactions, refunds, disputes)
Layer-Based Components
Align components with architectural layers:
Web Application:
  - Presentation Layer (web UI, API clients)
  - Application Layer (business logic, validation)
  - Data Layer (persistence, caching)
Capability-Based Components
Align components with system capabilities:
Analytics Platform:
  - Data Ingestion Component (collects data from sources)
  - Data Processing Component (transforms and cleans data)
  - Data Storage Component (manages data persistence)
  - Analytics Component (provides query and reporting)


11.2.3 Boundary Evaluation Checklist
Component cohesion: Does the component have a single, well-defined responsibility?
Interface clarity: Are the component’s interfaces well-defined and stable?
Dependency direction: Do dependencies flow in one clear direction?
Operational independence: Can the component be deployed and scaled independently?
Team ownership: Does a single team have clear ownership of the component?
Failure isolation: Does failure of this component minimize impact on other components?
Evolution potential: Can the component evolve without breaking other components?


11.2.4 Common Boundary Anti-Patterns
God Component: A single component that does everything - Symptoms: Thousands of lines of code, handles multiple domains - Problems: Difficult to test, deploy, and maintain - Solution: Split by domain or capability
Chatty Components: Components that make excessive calls to each other - Symptoms: High network traffic, tight coupling through frequent interactions - Problems: Poor performance, difficult to scale independently - Solution: Combine chatty components or redesign interaction patterns
Leaky Boundaries: Components that expose internal details through interfaces - Symptoms: APIs that expose data structures or implementation details - Problems: Tight coupling, difficult to evolve independently - Solution: Design abstract interfaces that hide implementation
Orphan Components: Components with unclear purpose or ownership - Symptoms: Unused code, unclear responsibilities - Problems: Maintenance burden, confusion for developers - Solution: Remove if unused, clarify purpose if needed

11.3 Component to Implementation Mapping
While the ontology defines components at the architectural level, implementations may map to various structures:
Component: User Service

Possible implementations:
  - Single monolithic service (Node.js, Express)
  - Microservice with multiple sub-services

title: 12  Interfaces and Contracts
text:
12.0.1 Interface — Interaction Point Entity
Components do not exist in isolation. Systems emerge from the interactions between components, and these interactions must occur through well-defined structural points. In the ontology, these interaction points are represented as interfaces.
Interfaces define the boundaries through which components communicate. They expose capabilities, define data exchange structures, and regulate interaction behavior. Without explicit interfaces, component dependencies become implicit and architectural structures become difficult to analyze.
Closely associated with interfaces are contracts. While interfaces define the interaction point, contracts define the rules governing that interaction. Together, interfaces and contracts form the foundation of system interoperability and architectural stability.
An interface represents a point of interaction between components or between a system and its external context.
Interfaces define how requests, events, or commands enter and exit components. They represent the formal connection points through which architectural elements communicate.
Interfaces typically expose several structural properties:
Interfaces may take different concrete forms depending on the architectural style of the system. Common examples include:
In the ontology, interfaces are represented as distinct entities rather than attributes of components. This separation allows interfaces to be referenced, versioned, and governed independently of the components that implement them.
Interfaces therefore function as the structural connectors of the system architecture.

title: 12  Interfaces and Contracts
text:
12.1 Interface Examples by Component Type

12.1.1 API Gateway Interfaces
API Gateway Component
├── Public User API (api)
│   - Endpoint: POST /api/users
│   - Purpose: Create new user accounts
│   - Contract: UserCreationRequest → UserResponse
│   - Version: v2
│
├── Public Order API (api)
│   - Endpoint: POST /api/orders
│   - Purpose: Submit new orders
│   - Contract: OrderCreationRequest → OrderResponse
│   - Version: v3
│
└── Internal Health Check API (api)
    - Endpoint: GET /health
    - Purpose: Service health monitoring
    - Contract: Empty → HealthStatus
    - Version: v1


12.1.2 Worker Component Interfaces
Data Processing Worker
├── Task Queue Interface (event)
│   - Topic: data_processing_tasks
│   - Purpose: Receive processing tasks
│   - Contract: ProcessingTask → TaskResult
│   - Version: v1
│
├── Progress Event Interface (event)
│   - Topic: processing_progress
│   - Purpose: Publish processing progress
│   - Contract: ProgressEvent → (consumed by monitoring)
│   - Version: v1
│
└── Completion Callback Interface (api)
    - Endpoint: POST /callback/completion
    - Purpose: Report task completion
    - Contract: CompletionRequest → CompletionResponse
    - Version: v1


12.1.3 Database Component Interfaces
Database Component
├── Query Interface (api)
│   - Protocol: JDBC/ODBC
│   - Purpose: Execute read queries
│   - Contract: SQL Query → ResultSet
│   - Version: N/A (protocol-defined)
│
├── Transaction Interface (api)
│   - Protocol: Database-specific
│   - Purpose: Begin, commit, rollback transactions
│   - Contract: TransactionOperation → TransactionResult
│   - Version: N/A (protocol-defined)
│
└── Change Data Capture Interface (event)
    - Topic: database_changes
    - Purpose: Emit data modification events
    - Contract: DataChangeEvent → (consumed by CDC consumers)
    - Version: v1


12.1.4 Interface Versioning
Interfaces are among the most stable elements of a system architecture. While internal component implementations may evolve frequently, interfaces often persist over long periods because they define integration boundaries between systems.
For this reason, interface versioning becomes a key mechanism for managing architectural evolution.
When an interface changes in ways that may affect compatibility, a new version must be introduced. Version identifiers allow multiple interface definitions to coexist while clients gradually migrate to newer versions.
Interface versioning serves several architectural functions.
First, it provides a stable reference point for system integrations. External systems can depend on a specific interface version without being affected by internal system changes.
Second, versioning enables incremental evolution of system architecture. New capabilities can be introduced through new interface versions while maintaining compatibility with existing integrations.
Third, interface versions function as historical markers of system architecture. By examining interface evolution over time, it becomes possible to analyze how a system’s structure and capabilities have changed.
Within the ontology, interfaces therefore carry explicit version identifiers and version relationships. These relationships capture how interface definitions evolve across system releases.
Through this mechanism, interface versioning becomes a central index of architectural change.

title: 12  Interfaces and Contracts
text:
12.2 Interface Versioning Strategies

12.2.1 Strategy 1: URI Versioning
Version is embedded in the interface URI:
Version 1: /api/v1/users
Version 2: /api/v2/users
Version 3: /api/v3/users

Advantages:
  - Clear separation between versions
  - Easy to route requests to appropriate handlers
  - Can deprecate old versions by removing endpoints

Disadvantages:
  - URI changes require client updates
  - Version is exposed in client code
  - Multiple versions increase API surface area


12.2.2 Strategy 2: Header Versioning
Version is specified in request headers:
Endpoint: /api/users
Header: API-Version: v1

Version 1 Request:
  GET /api/users
  API-Version: v1

Version 2 Request:
  GET /api/users
  API-Version: v2

Advantages:
  - Clean URIs without version information
  - Same endpoint can handle multiple versions
  - Version can be negotiated dynamically

Disadvantages:
  - Less discoverable
  - Requires header support in all clients
  - Harder to cache responses


12.2.3 Strategy 3: Content Negotiation
Version is specified via content negotiation:
Accept header specifies version:
  Accept: application/vnd.api.v1+json
  Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json

Advantages:
  - HTTP-standard approach
  - Can negotiate other aspects simultaneously (format, language)
  - Clean separation of concerns

Disadvantages:
  - Complex to implement
  - Requires content negotiation support
  - Not all clients support this pattern

title: 12  Interfaces and Contracts
text:
12.3 Interface Evolution Patterns

12.3.1 Additive Changes (Compatible)
Adding new fields or operations without breaking existing functionality:
Original Interface (v1):
  POST /api/users
  Request: { "name": "string", "email": "string" }
  Response: { "user_id": "string", "name": "string", "email": "string" }

Evolved Interface (v2):
  POST /api/users
  Request: { "name": "string", "email": "string", "phone": "string" }
  Response: { "user_id": "string", "name": "string", "email": "string", "phone": "string" }

Strategy:
  - Keep v1 interface unchanged
  - Introduce v2 with additional fields
  - v1 requests ignore new fields
  - Gradually migrate clients to v2


12.3.2 Non-Breaking Modifications (Compatible)
Changing interface semantics without breaking existing clients:
Original Interface (v1):
  POST /api/orders
  Behavior: Creates order synchronously

Evolved Interface (v2):
  POST /api/orders
  Behavior: Creates order asynchronously, returns job ID
  New Endpoint: GET /api/orders/{job_id}
  Purpose: Check order creation status

Strategy:
  - v2 provides enhanced async behavior
  - v1 clients continue to work with synchronous mode
  - New clients can use async mode for better performance


12.3.3 Breaking Changes (New Version Required)
Changes that require clients to be updated:
Original Interface (v1):
  GET /api/users/{id}
  Response: { "user_id": "string", "name": "string", "email": "string" }

Breaking Change (v2):
  GET /api/users/{id}
  Response: { "user_id": "string", "full_name": "string", "contact_email": "string" }

Strategy:
  - Maintain v1 interface alongside v2
  - Document migration path from v1 to v2
  - Set deprecation date for v1 (e.g., 6 months)
  - Monitor v1 usage before removal
  - Remove v1 after migration period

title: 12  Interfaces and Contracts
text:
12.4 Interface Lifecycle Management

12.4.1 Version Introduction

Design - Define new interface version with clear contract
Implement - Deploy new version alongside existing versions
Document - Provide migration guide and examples
Announce - Notify users of new version availability
Monitor - Track adoption and usage patterns



12.4.2 Version Deprecation

Announce Deprecation - Publish deprecation notice with timeline
Provide Migration Guide - Offer clear steps for migrating to newer version
Add Warnings - Return deprecation warnings in responses
Monitor Usage - Track remaining clients using deprecated version
Schedule Removal - Set final removal date



12.4.3 Version Removal

Verify Migration - Confirm no active clients using deprecated version
Remove Endpoint - Delete deprecated interface implementation
Update Documentation - Remove deprecated version from docs
Clean Up Tests - Remove tests for deprecated version
Archive Specifications - Keep record of removed versions for reference

title: 12  Interfaces and Contracts
text:
12.5 Interface Versioning Best Practices
Use Semantic Versioning - MAJOR version: Breaking changes - MINOR version: Additive changes - PATCH version: Bug fixes, documentation updates
Maintain Backward Compatibility - Prefer additive changes over breaking changes - Use default values for new fields - Support both old and new request formats when possible
Document Version Changes - Maintain changelog for each version - Provide migration guides - Include example requests/responses - Document deprecation timelines
Monitor Version Usage - Track which versions clients are using - Set up alerts for deprecated version usage - Gather feedback on new versions - Analyze migration patterns
Plan Deprecation Carefully - Provide ample migration time (typically 6-12 months) - Offer direct support for migration - Consider grandfather clauses for long-term clients - Communicate deprecation early and frequently

title: 13  Data Entities and State
text:
13.0.1 Data Entity — Business Entities vs Technical Entities
Software systems exist not only to perform computation but also to create, transform, store, and transmit data. Data therefore occupies a central role in architectural representation. Components process data, workflows move data between components, and system behavior often depends on the state encoded in stored information.
For this reason, the ontology treats data entities and state as first-class elements of system architecture. Explicitly representing data structures and their lifecycle allows system architectures to be analyzed in terms of data ownership, flow patterns, and persistence boundaries.
A Data Entity represents a structured unit of information managed by a system.
Data entities capture the logical structures through which information is represented, stored, and exchanged. They may correspond to domain concepts, operational records, or technical artifacts used internally by the system.
Two categories of data entities are particularly important.
Business Entities
Business entities represent domain concepts that are meaningful within the problem domain of the system. These entities correspond to real-world objects, processes, or relationships that the system models.
Examples may include:
Business entities typically form the conceptual core of the system’s data model. Their structure often remains stable even as implementation technologies change.
Technical Entities
Technical entities represent data structures created for operational or infrastructural purposes. These entities support system execution rather than representing domain concepts.
Examples may include:
While business entities model domain reality, technical entities support system functionality.
Distinguishing between these categories helps clarify the role of different data structures within system architecture.

title: 13  Data Entities and State
13  Data Entities and State
text:
13.3 Data Flow Patterns

13.3.1 Request-Response Data Flow
Client Request → Component A (reads cache) → [cache miss] → Component B (reads database) → Response
                  ↓
              [writes to cache]

Characteristics:
  - Synchronous interaction
  - Client waits for response
  - Often includes caching layers
  - Used in web applications and APIs


13.3.2 Event-Driven Data Flow
Component A (emits event) → Message Broker → Component B (consumes event)
                                        ↓
                                   Component C (consumes event)
                                        ↓
                                   Component D (consumes event)

Characteristics:
  - Asynchronous interaction
  - Producers don't know consumers
  - Multiple consumers possible
  - Loose coupling between components


13.3.3 Pipeline Data Flow
Input Data → Stage 1 (transform) → Stage 2 (transform) → Stage 3 (transform) → Output Data

Characteristics:
  - Sequential data transformation
  - Each stage processes data in order
  - Often used in data processing systems
  - Can be batch or streaming


13.3.4 Fan-Out/Fan-In Data Flow
Component A → Component B → Component E (aggregates)
            → Component C →
            → Component D →

Characteristics:
  - Parallel processing of same data
  - Results aggregated later
  - Used for distributed computation
  - Improves performance for independent operations


13.3.5 Broadcast Data Flow
Component A (publishes) → Component B (subscribes)
                     → Component C (subscribes)
                     → Component D (subscribes)

Characteristics:
  - One producer, multiple consumers
  - Same data sent to all consumers
  - Used for notifications and events
  - Loose coupling between publisher and subscribers

title: 13  Data Entities and State
text:
13.4 State Management Patterns

13.4.1 Stateless Component Pattern
Component processes requests without maintaining internal state:
  - All state stored externally (database, cache)
  - Requests are independent
  - Easy to scale horizontally
  - No session affinity required

Example: Stateless API Service
  - Request contains all needed context
  - Database stores all persistent data
  - Redis stores temporary session data
  - Multiple instances can handle any request


13.4.2 Stateful Component Pattern
Component maintains internal state:
  - State persists across requests
  - Session affinity may be required
  - More complex to scale
  - Lower latency for state-dependent operations

Example: Stateful Workflow Engine
  - Maintains workflow execution state
  - Tracks progress across multiple steps
  - Coordinates complex business processes
  - May require sticky sessions


13.4.3 Caching Layer Pattern
Cache layer reduces load on persistent storage:
  - Frequently accessed data cached
  - Reduces latency
  - Improves throughput
  - Introduces consistency challenges

Example: Read-Through Cache
  - Component A requests data
  - Cache checked first
  - Cache miss → fetch from database
  - Result stored in cache
  - Subsequent requests served from cache


13.4.4 Event Sourcing Pattern
State derived from sequence of events:
  - All state changes recorded as events
  - Current state computed from event history
  - Enables audit trails and replay
  - Different from CRUD operations

Example: Order System with Event Sourcing
  - Events: OrderCreated, PaymentReceived, OrderShipped
  - Current order state computed from events
  - Can reconstruct state at any point in time
  - Supports event-driven architecture

title: 14  Workflow and Execution Units
text:
14.0.1 Workflow — Orchestration Structure
While components define the structural elements of a system, workflows define how these elements cooperate to produce behavior. Workflows represent the orchestration logic that coordinates tasks, data flows, and component interactions over time.
In many modern systems, particularly distributed systems and data pipelines, behavior emerges not from isolated component operations but from structured sequences of execution. These sequences determine how work progresses through the system, which components participate in processing, and how results are produced.
The ontology therefore treats workflows and execution units as explicit entities within the architectural representation.
A Workflow represents a structured sequence of operations that collectively accomplish a system objective.
Workflows coordinate tasks across components, defining the order in which operations occur and the conditions under which they proceed. They often represent the operational realization of system capabilities.
A workflow may include several structural elements:
Workflows appear in many forms across system architectures. Examples include:
Within the ontology, workflows capture the behavioral coordination layer of the system.

title: 14  Workflow and Execution Units
text:
14.1 Workflow Examples

14.1.1 Example 1: Order Processing Workflow
Workflow: Order Processing
Trigger: OrderCreatedEvent

Steps:
  1. Validate Order
     - Checks inventory availability
     - Validates payment method
     - Branch: If inventory unavailable → OutOfStockError
             If payment invalid → PaymentError
  
  2. Process Payment
     - Charges payment method
     - Branch: If payment failed → PaymentError
             If payment succeeded → continue
  
  3. Update Inventory
     - Reserves ordered items
     - Updates stock levels
  
  4. Generate Confirmation
     - Creates order confirmation
     - Sends email to customer
  
  5. Schedule Fulfillment
     - Creates fulfillment task
     - Notifies warehouse

Error Handling:
  - OutOfStockError → Notify customer, cancel order
  - PaymentError → Retry payment (3 attempts), then cancel

Termination:
  - Success: Order completed, confirmation sent
  - Failure: Order cancelled, customer notified


14.1.2 Example 2: Data Ingestion Workflow
Workflow: Data Ingestion Pipeline
Trigger: Scheduled (daily at 2 AM)

Steps:
  1. Fetch Data
     - Connect to external data source
     - Download data files
  
  2. Validate Schema
     - Validate data structure
     - Branch: If invalid → SchemaError
             If valid → continue
  
  3. Transform Data
     - Apply business rules
     - Normalize formats
  
  4. Deduplicate
     - Remove duplicate records
     - Maintain data quality
  
  5. Load to Warehouse
     - Insert into data warehouse
     - Update indexes
  
  6. Generate Report
     - Create ingestion summary
     - Send to operations team

Error Handling:
  - SchemaError → Alert data team, pause ingestion
  - ConnectionError → Retry (5 attempts), then escalate

Termination:
  - Success: Data loaded, report generated
  - Failure: Partial load possible, report errors


14.1.3 Example 3: Agent Tool-Calling Workflow
Workflow: Task Execution
Trigger: User Task Request

Steps:
  1. Analyze Task
     - Parse user request
     - Identify required capabilities
  
  2. Plan Actions
     - Generate step-by-step plan
     - Select required tools
  
  3. Execute Step 1
     - Invoke Tool A
     - Capture result
  
  4. Evaluate Progress
     - Check if step completed successfully
     - Branch: If failed → Retry or adjust plan
             If succeeded → continue
  
  5. Execute Step 2 (if needed)
     - Invoke Tool B
     - Capture result
  
  6. Evaluate Progress
     - Check if step completed successfully
     - Branch: If failed → Retry or adjust plan
             If succeeded → continue
  
  7. Continue Steps 3-N
     - Repeat for remaining steps
  
  8. Synthesize Results
     - Combine all step results
     - Generate final response

Error Handling:
  - Tool failure → Retry (3 attempts), then skip or use alternative
  - Execution timeout → Terminate workflow, report partial results

Termination:
  - Success: All steps completed, final response generated
  - Failure: Partial completion, report what was achieved


14.1.4 Example 4: Image Processing Workflow
Workflow: Image Processing Pipeline
Trigger: ImageUploadEvent

Steps:
  1. Receive Image
     - Accept uploaded image file
     - Validate file format and size
  
  2. Generate Thumbnails
     - Create multiple thumbnail sizes
     - Parallel execution:
       - Small thumbnail (100x100)
       - Medium thumbnail (300x300)
       - Large thumbnail (600x600)
  
  3. Apply Watermark
     - Add branding watermark
     - Position in bottom-right corner
  
  4. Optimize for Web
     - Compress image
     - Adjust quality settings
  
  5. Store Variants
     - Save original image
     - Save all thumbnails
     - Store metadata
  
  6. Update Database
     - Record image details
     - Update user statistics

Error Handling:
  - Invalid file → Reject upload, notify user
  - Processing failure → Retry (2 attempts), then mark as failed

Termination:
  - Success: All variants created and stored
  - Failure: Original preserved, partial variants created

text:

title: 14  Workflow and Execution Units
text:
14.3 Execution Granularity Hierarchy
Workflow (highest level)
  └── Represents complete business process
  └── Coordinates multiple jobs or steps
  └── Example: "Order Processing Workflow"

Job (execution instance)
  └── Represents single workflow execution
  └── Contains specific parameters and context
  └── Example: "Order #12345 Processing Job"

Task (functional operation)
  └── Represents discrete unit of work
  └── Performed by specific component
  └── Example: "Validate Payment Task"

Step (workflow stage)
  └── Represents ordered stage in workflow
  └── Defines execution sequence
  └── Example: "Step 3: Process Payment"

Function (lowest level)
  └── Represents code-level operation
  └── Implementation detail
  └── Example: "validatePaymentMethod()"

title: 14  Workflow and Execution Units
text:
14.4 Runtime Topology Examples

14.4.1 Simple Web Application Runtime
Runtime Topology: Web Application

Deployment:
  - Web UI: 2 instances behind load balancer
  - API Service: 3 instances behind load balancer
  - Database: 1 primary + 2 read replicas

Scaling:
  - Web UI: Auto-scale 2-5 instances based on CPU
  - API Service: Auto-scale 3-8 instances based on request rate
  - Database: Read replicas scale based on query load

Distribution:
  - All components deployed in same region
  - Network latency between components <10ms
  - Shared network for internal communication


14.4.2 Distributed Data Pipeline Runtime
Runtime Topology: Data Pipeline

Deployment:
  - Ingestion Workers: 10 instances across availability zones
  - Transformation Engine: 5 instances with GPU acceleration
  - Storage Cluster: Distributed object storage
  - Analytics Engine: 3 instances for query processing

Scaling:
  - Ingestion: Scale based on incoming data volume
  - Transformation: Scale based on queue depth
  - Analytics: Scale based on query load

Distribution:
  - Components distributed across 3 availability zones
  - Data replicated for durability
  - Regional deployment for latency optimization


14.4.3 Multi-Region Service Runtime
Runtime Topology: Global API Service

Deployment:
  - Region US-East: 5 API instances, 2 database replicas
  - Region US-West: 4 API instances, 2 database replicas
  - Region EU-West: 4 API instances, 2 database replicas

Scaling:
  - Each region scales independently
  - Global load balancer routes requests
  - Automatic failover between regions

Distribution:
  - Database master in primary region
  - Read replicas in all regions
  - Cross-region replication for consistency
  - DNS-based traffic routing



14.4.4 Task, Job, and Step — Execution Granularity
Execution within a workflow occurs through smaller operational units. These units represent the granularity of work performed during system execution.
Three related concepts appear frequently in system architectures.
A Task represents a discrete unit of work performed by a component. Tasks correspond to specific operations such as processing a request, executing a computation, or transforming data.
A Job represents a larger execution instance composed of one or more tasks. Jobs often correspond to scheduled processes, batch computations, or background operations.
A Step represents an individual stage within a workflow. Steps define the order in which tasks are executed and often correspond to logical stages in a processing pipeline.
These execution units form a hierarchy of granularity:

workflows coordinate execution structures
jobs represent runtime execution instances
tasks perform functional operations
steps define ordered execution within workflows

The ontology allows these units to be represented explicitly so that system behavior can be described in terms of execution structure rather than only component relationships.


14.4.5 Trigger — Initiating Execution
Workflows and jobs do not execute continuously. Their execution is initiated by triggers.
A Trigger represents the condition that causes a workflow or task to begin execution. Triggers connect system behavior to external events, internal signals, or scheduled conditions.
Three categories of triggers commonly appear in system architectures.
Time-based triggers
Time-based triggers initiate workflows according to scheduled intervals or specific timestamps. These triggers are commonly used in batch processing systems, maintenance operations, and periodic data synchronization tasks.
Event-based triggers
Event-based triggers initiate execution when a specific event occurs. Events may originate from external systems, message brokers, or internal components. Event-driven architectures rely heavily on this form of trigger.
Request-based triggers
Request-based triggers originate from direct interactions with system interfaces. Examples include API calls, user actions, or command invocations.
Triggers therefore connect system workflows to the broader system environment.


14.4.6 Runtime — Execution Topology
While workflows describe the logical coordination of execution, systems ultimately operate within runtime environments.
The runtime topology represents how components, workflows, and execution units are arranged during system operation. It describes where execution occurs and how runtime resources are allocated.
Runtime topology may include elements such as:

service instances
worker pools
container deployments
distributed processing nodes
orchestration controllers

Understanding runtime topology is important because architectural behavior often depends on runtime structure. Performance characteristics, reliability properties, and scaling behavior all emerge from the runtime configuration of system components.
Within the ontology, runtime entities provide the foundation for later architectural projections such as deployment views, operations views, and runtime observability models.
By linking workflows, execution units, triggers, and runtime topology, the ontology captures the operational dimension of system architecture, complementing the structural representation defined by components and interfaces.

title: 15  Relation Types (v0.1)
text:
15.0.1 contains / part_of — Structural Composition
Entities alone cannot describe system architecture. A collection of components, interfaces, and data entities becomes meaningful only when the relationships between them are explicitly defined.
Relations capture how architectural elements are connected. They describe structural containment, operational dependencies, communication paths, data access patterns, and responsibility boundaries. When entities are connected through well-defined relations, the ontology forms a system structure graph.
The relation set defined in Ontology v0.1 is intentionally minimal. It includes only the relations necessary to represent the structural and operational interactions commonly observed in software systems.
The contains and part_of relations describe structural composition.
These relations represent hierarchical relationships between architectural entities. They indicate that one entity is structurally included within another.
Typical examples include:
The relation contains expresses the forward direction of composition, while part_of expresses the inverse relationship.
Structural composition establishes the hierarchical organization of systems and allows complex architectures to be represented as nested structures.

title: 15  Relation Types (v0.1)
text:
15.1 Relation Examples

15.1.1 Composition Relations
System Composition:
  E-commerce System contains:
    - Web UI
    - API Service
    - Database
    - Payment Gateway
    - Email Service

Workflow Composition:
  Order Processing Workflow contains:
    - Step 1: Validate Order
    - Step 2: Process Payment
    - Step 3: Update Inventory
    - Step 4: Generate Confirmation
    - Step 5: Send Email

Data Composition:
  Order Data contains:
    - Order ID
    - User ID
    - Order Items (array)
    - Total Amount
    - Shipping Address
    - Billing Address


15.1.2 Dependency Relations
Service Dependencies:
  Order Service depends_on:
    - Database (for order persistence)
    - Payment Gateway (for payment processing)
    - Inventory Service (for stock verification)
    - Email Service (for confirmations)

Component Dependencies:
  Web UI depends_on:
    - API Service (for data retrieval)
    - CDN (for asset delivery)
    
Workflow Dependencies:
  Ingestion Pipeline depends_on:
    - Data Source (external system)
    - Transformation Engine (internal component)
    - Data Warehouse (storage destination)


15.1.3 Invocation Relations
Synchronous Invocation:
  Web UI calls API Service:
    - HTTP POST /api/orders
    - Waits for response
    - Handles result or error
    
Workflow Invocation:
  Workflow Engine invokes Task Worker:
    - Triggers task execution
    - Monitors completion
    - Handles success/failure
    
Internal Invocation:
  API Service calls Authentication Service:
    - Validates user token
    - Returns user permissions
    - Synchronous call


15.1.4 Event Relations
Event Emission:
  Order Service emits:
    - OrderCreated event
    - PaymentCompleted event
    - OrderShipped event

Event Consumption:
  Inventory Service consumes OrderCreated event:
    - Reserves inventory
    - Updates stock levels
    
Email Service consumes OrderShipped event:
    - Sends shipping notification
    - Updates customer communication log
    
Analytics Service consumes all events:
    - Aggregates metrics
    - Generates reports


15.1.5 Data Access Relations
Read Relations:
  Order Service reads:
    - User Data (from User Database)
    - Product Data (from Product Database)
    - Inventory Data (from Inventory Database)
    
Analytics Engine reads:
    - Transaction Records (from Data Warehouse)
    - User Behavior Logs (from Event Store)

Write Relations:
  Order Service writes:
    - Order Records (to Order Database)
    - Transaction Records (to Transaction Database)
    
Ingestion Worker writes:
    - Raw Data (to Data Lake)
    - Processed Data (to Data Warehouse)


15.1.6 Governance Relations
Ownership Relations:
  Payments Team owns:
    - Payment Service
    - Transaction Database
    - Fraud Detection System
    
Operations Team owns:
    - Monitoring Infrastructure
    - Alert Management System
    - Incident Response Tools

Governance Relations:
  Security Policy governs:
    - Authentication mechanisms
    - Access control rules
    - Data encryption requirements
    
Compliance Policy governs:
    - Data retention policies
    - Audit logging requirements
    - Privacy protection measures


15.1.7 Contract Relations
Implementation Relations:
  Order Service implements:
    - Order API Interface
    - Order Processing Interface
    
Payment Service implements:
    - Payment API Interface
    - Transaction Interface

Conformance Relations:
  Order API conforms_to:
    - REST API Specification
    - JSON Schema Definition
    - Rate Limiting Policy
    
Event Stream conforms_to:
    - Event Schema Definition
    - Serialization Format
    - Delivery Guarantees

│  │  Stage 2 │──────│  Stage 3 │                │
│  └──────────┘      └──────────┘               │
│       │                    │                   │
│       ↓                    ↓                   │
│  ┌──────────┐          ┌──────────┐            │
│  │ Storage  │          │Analytics │            │
│  │ Warehouse│          │  Engine  │            │
│  └──────────┘          └──────────┘            │
│                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Relations:
  Ingest Stage reads from external sources
  Ingest Stage writes to Transform Stage 1
  Transform Stage 1 writes to Transform Stage 2
  Transform Stage 2 writes to Transform Stage 3 (parallel)
  Transform Stage 2 and 3 write to Storage Warehouse
  Analytics Engine reads from Storage Warehouse



15.2.4 depends_on — Dependency Relationships
The depends_on relation represents a dependency between entities.
A dependency indicates that one entity requires the presence or functionality of another entity in order to operate correctly.
Examples include:

a service component depends_on a database component
a worker process depends_on a message queue
a processing pipeline depends_on a configuration store

Dependency relations are directional. The source entity requires the target entity for correct operation.
Explicitly representing dependencies enables architectural analysis of coupling, reliability risks, and failure propagation paths.


15.2.5 calls / invokes — Invocation Relationships
The calls or invokes relation represents a direct execution request between components.
This relation captures synchronous or directed interactions in which one component requests an operation from another component through an interface.
Typical examples include:

a web service calls an internal API service
a workflow engine invokes a task processor
an application component invokes a computation engine

Invocation relations are typically associated with request-response interaction patterns.
Distinguishing invocation relations from general dependencies allows the ontology to capture dynamic execution paths within the system.


15.2.6 emits / consumes — Event Relationships
The emits and consumes relations represent asynchronous communication through events.
In event-driven architectures, components publish events that may be processed by other components. This interaction pattern differs from direct invocation because the producer does not necessarily know which consumers will process the event.
Examples include:

a transaction service emits an event when an order is created
a notification service consumes that event to generate alerts
an analytics pipeline consumes event streams for processing

Event relations represent loosely coupled communication structures and are fundamental to event-driven system architectures.


15.2.7 reads / writes — Data Access Relationships
The reads and writes relations represent interactions between components and data entities.
These relations capture how components access and modify system data.
Examples include:

a service component reads user profile data
a processing engine writes transaction records
an analytics pipeline reads historical data from storage

Data access relations are important for understanding data ownership, data flow patterns, and consistency constraints within system architectures.


15.2.8 owns / governs — Responsibility Relationships
Not all relations describe technical interactions. Some relations represent organizational or operational responsibility.
The owns and governs relations represent responsibility assignments between stakeholders and architectural entities.
Examples include:

a team owns a service component
an operations group governs infrastructure resources
a policy authority governs security constraints

Responsibility relations connect the technical architecture to the organizational structures that operate and maintain it.
These relations are particularly important for understanding operational accountability and system governance.


15.2.9 implements / conforms_to — Implementation and Contract Relationships
The implements and conforms_to relations describe how components satisfy defined interfaces or contracts.
A component implements an interface when it provides the operational behavior defined by that interface.
Similarly, a component conforms_to a contract when its behavior satisfies the rules defined by a data schema, protocol specification, or policy definition.
Examples include:

a service component implements an API interface
an event processor conforms_to an event schema
a system component conforms_to a security policy

These relations connect structural elements to the contracts that govern their behavior.

Together, these relation types form the minimal relational vocabulary required to represent system architecture. By combining entities with these relations, the ontology constructs a structured graph that captures the essential dependencies, interactions, and responsibilities of software systems.

15.3.4 Relation Usage Quick Reference

│                        RELATION USAGE QUICK REFERENCE                                    │

│                                                                                         │
│ WHEN TO USE...                                                                        │
│                                                                                         │
│ contains / part_of:                                                                   │
│   ✓ When one entity is structurally included in another                                │

│   ✓ For workflow steps (Workflow → Step)                                               │
