│                                                                                         │
│ depends_on:                                                                            │
│   ✓ When one entity cannot function without another                                     │
│   ✓ For dependencies that are not invocations                                           │
│   ✓ For external service dependencies                                                   │
│   Example: OrderService depends_on PaymentGateway                                       │
│                                                                                         │
│ calls / invokes:                                                                       │
│   ✓ When one entity directly invokes another's operations                               │
│   ✓ For synchronous invocations (HTTP, gRPC)                                           │
│   ✓ For direct method calls                                                            │
│   Example: OrderService calls PaymentService.processPayment()                            │
│                                                                                         │
│ emits / consumes:                                                                      │
│   ✓ When entities communicate through events                                            │
│   ✓ For asynchronous messaging                                                         │
│   ✓ For event-driven architectures                                                      │
│   Example: DataIngestionService emits DataReceivedEvent                                  │
│                                                                                         │
│ reads / writes:                                                                         │
│   ✓ When components access data entities                                                │
│   ✓ For database operations                                                            │
│   ✓ For file system access                                                             │
│   Example: ProductService reads Product from ProductDatabase                             │
│                                                                                         │
│ owns:                                                                                  │
│   ✓ When a component has ownership of data                                             │
│   ✓ For data ownership and responsibility                                               │
│   ✓ For lifecycle management                                                           │
│   Example: ProductService owns Product data entity                                      │
│                                                                                         │
│ implements:                                                                            │
│   ✓ When a component provides a capability                                              │
│   ✓ When a component implements an interface                                            │
│   ✓ For capability realization                                                         │
│   Example: ProductService implements ProductCatalog capability                          │
│                                                                                         │
│ provides / exposes:                                                                    │
│   ✓ When a component provides an interface                                             │
│   ✓ When an interface exposes a capability                                             │
│   ✓ For API definitions                                                                │
│   Example: ProductService provides ProductAPI                                           │
│                                                                                         │
│ orchestrated_by / involves:                                                            │
│   ✓ For workflow definitions                                                           │
│   ✓ For workflow execution                                                            │
│   ✓ For process coordination                                                           │
│   Example: OrderWorkflow orchestrated_by OrderService                                   │
│                                                                                         │
│ applies_to:                                                                            │
│   ✓ When a constraint applies to an entity                                             │
│   ✓ For quality attribute constraints                                                   │
│   ✓ For policy enforcement                                                             │
│   Example: PerformanceConstraint applies_to OrderService                                │
│                                                                                         │
│ mitigates:                                                                             │
│   ✓ When a reliability hook addresses a failure mode                                  │
│   ✓ For fault tolerance mechanisms                                                     │
│   ✓ For resilience patterns                                                            │
│   Example: RetryHook mitigates NetworkFailure                                          │
│                                                                                         │
│ enforces:                                                                              │
│   ✓ When a security hook enforces a policy                                             │
│   ✓ For access control                                                                 │
│   ✓ For compliance enforcement                                                         │
│   Example: AuthenticationHook enforces AccessControl                                    │
│                                                                                         │
│ separates:                                                                             │
│   ✓ When a trust boundary separates security domains                                    │
│   ✓ For security zones                                                                │
│   ✓ For privilege boundaries                                                           │
│   Example: NetworkBoundary separates ExternalNetwork from InternalNetwork               │


15.3.5 Common Relation Patterns
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                          COMMON RELATION PATTERNS                                         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                                         │
│ PATTERN 1: System-Component-Interface Chain                                            │
│                                                                                         │
│   System → contains → Component → provides → Interface → exposes → Capability          │
│                                                                                         │
│   Example:                                                                              │
│     EcommercePlatform contains ProductService                                          │
│     ProductService provides ProductAPI                                                  │
│     ProductAPI exposes ProductCatalog                                                   │
│                                                                                         │
│ PATTERN 2: Component-Dependency-Call Chain                                             │
│                                                                                         │
│   Component → depends_on → Component → calls → Component                                │
│                                                                                         │
│   Example:                                                                              │
│     OrderService depends_on PaymentService                                              │
│     OrderService calls PaymentService.processPayment()                                   │
│                                                                                         │
│ PATTERN 3: Component-Data-Access Chain                                                 │
│                                                                                         │
│   Component → owns → Data Entity ← reads/writes ← Component                             │
│                                                                                         │
│   Example:                                                                              │
│     ProductService owns Product                                                        │
│     ProductService reads Product from ProductDatabase                                   │
│     OrderService writes Order to OrderDatabase                                          │
│                                                                                         │
│ PATTERN 4: Event-Driven Chain                                                          │
│                                                                                         │
│   Component → emits → Interface ← consumes → Component                                   │
│                                                                                         │
│   Example:                                                                              │
│     DataIngestionService emits DataReceivedEvent                                        │
│     DataTransformationService consumes DataReceivedEvent                                 │
│                                                                                         │
│ PATTERN 5: Workflow-Orchestration Chain                                                 │
│                                                                                         │
│   Workflow → orchestrated_by → Component → involves → Component                          │
│                                                                                         │
│   Example:                                                                              │
│     OrderWorkflow orchestrated_by OrderService                                          │
│     OrderWorkflow involves [ProductService, PaymentService]                             │
│                                                                                         │
│ PATTERN 6: Constraint-Application Chain                                                 │
│                                                                                         │
│   Constraint → applies_to → Component → conforms_to → Constraint                         │
│                                                                                         │
│   Example:                                                                              │
│     PerformanceConstraint applies_to OrderService                                       │
│     OrderService conforms_to PerformanceConstraint                                      │
│                                                                                         │
│ PATTERN 7: Failure-Mitigation Chain                                                     │
│                                                                                         │
│   Failure Mode → affected_by → Component ← mitigates ← Reliability Hook                 │
│                                                                                         │
│   Example:                                                                              │
│     NetworkFailure affects OrderService                                                 │
│     RetryHook mitigates NetworkFailure                                                  │
│                                                                                         │
│ PATTERN 8: Security-Enforcement Chain                                                   │
│                                                                                         │
│   Security Hook → enforces → Policy → conforms_to → Component                            │
│                                                                                         │
│   Example:                                                                              │
│     AuthenticationHook enforces AccessPolicy                                            │
│     OrderService conforms_to AccessPolicy                                               │
│                                                                                         │
│ PATTERN 9: Trust Boundary Chain                                                         │
│                                                                                         │
│   Trust Boundary → separates → Component → protected_by → Security Hook                  │
│                                                                                         │
│   Example:                                                                              │
│     NetworkBoundary separates ExternalNetwork from InternalNetwork                       │
│     InternalNetwork protected_by AuthenticationHook                                     │
│                                                                                         │
│ PATTERN 10: Capability-Implementation Chain                                            │
│                                                                                         │
│   Capability → implemented_by → Component → implements → Capability                     │
│                                                                                         │
│   Example:                                                                              │
│     ProductCatalog implemented by ProductService                                        │
│     ProductService implements ProductCatalog                                             │


15.3.6 Relation Cardinality Guidelines
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         RELATION CARDINALITY GUIDELINES                                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                                         │
│ Relation          │ Expected Cardinality │ Notes                                         │
├───────────────────┼───────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ contains          │ 1:N                   │ One entity contains many entities            │
│ part_of           │ N:1                   │ Many entities are part of one entity        │
│ depends_on        │ 1:N or N:1            │ Can be one-to-many or many-to-one           │
│ calls             │ 1:N or N:1            │ Can be one-to-many or many-to-one           │
│ invokes           │ 1:N                   │ One entity invokes many operations           │
│ emits             │ 1:N                   │ One entity emits many events                 │
│ consumes          │ N:1                   │ Many entities consume one event              │
│ reads             │ 1:N                   │ One entity reads many data entities          │
│ writes            │ 1:N                   │ One entity writes many data entities         │
│ owns              │ 1:N                   │ One entity owns many data entities           │
│ implements        │ N:M                   │ Many components implement many capabilities   │
│ provides          │ 1:N                   │ One component provides many interfaces       │
│ exposes           │ 1:N                   │ One interface exposes many capabilities      │
│ orchestrated_by   │ N:1                   │ Many workflows orchestrated by one component │
│ involves          │ N:M                   │ Workflow involves many components            │
│ applies_to        │ N:M                   │ Constraint applies to many entities          │
│ mitigates         │ N:1                   │ Hook mitigates one failure mode              │
│ enforces          │ N:1                   │ Hook enforces one policy                     │
│ separates         │ N:N                   │ Boundary separates many entities              │
└───────────────────┴───────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Notes:
  • 1:N = One-to-many relationship
  • N:1 = Many-to-one relationship
  • N:M = Many-to-many relationship
  • Cardinality can vary based on specific use cases
  • Use appropriate cardinality for accurate modeling


15.3.7 Relation Validation Rules
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                          RELATION VALIDATION RULES                                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                                         │
│ RULE 1: Type Compatibility                                                              │
│   ✓ Source entity type must support the relation                                        │
│   ✓ Target entity type must be compatible with the relation                             │
│   ✗ Example: System cannot "calls" another System (use depends_on instead)             │
│                                                                                         │
│ RULE 2: Bidirectional Consistency                                                       │
│   ✓ If A contains B, then B part_of A                                                   │
│   ✓ If A emits event, then event consumed by B                                           │
│   ✗ Example: A contains B but B does not have part_of A (inconsistent)                 │
│                                                                                         │
│ RULE 3: No Circular Composition                                                         │
│   ✓ Avoid circular contains/part_of relationships                                      │
│   ✗ Example: A contains B, B contains C, C contains A (circular)                       │
│                                                                                         │
│ RULE 4: Dependency Acyclicity                                                           │
│   ✓ Avoid circular depends_on relationships                                             │
│   ✗ Example: A depends_on B, B depends_on C, C depends_on A (circular)                 │
│                                                                                         │
│ RULE 5: Interface Implementation                                                         │
│   ✓ Component implements interface must provide interface operations                    │
│   ✗ Example: Component implements interface but missing operations                     │
│                                                                                         │
│ RULE 6: Data Ownership                                                                  │
│   ✓ Data entity should have at most one owner                                           │
│   ✗ Example: Data entity owned by multiple components (ambiguous)                      │
│                                                                                         │
│ RULE 7: Constraint Applicability                                                        │
│   ✓ Constraint must apply to compatible entity types                                     │
│   ✗ Example: Security constraint applies to data entity (type mismatch)                │
│                                                                                         │
│ RULE 8: Workflow Orchestration                                                          │
│   ✓ Workflow must have valid orchestrator component                                     │
│   ✗ Example: Workflow orchestrated_by non-existent component                            │
│                                                                                         │
│ RULE 9: Event Semantics                                                                │
│   ✓ Event interface must have defined events                                            │
│   ✗ Example: Component emits event from non-event interface                             │
│                                                                                         │
│ RULE 10: Trust Boundary Separation                                                      │
│   ✓ Trust boundary must separate distinct security domains                              │
│   ✗ Example: Trust boundary separates entities in same domain (no separation)         │

title: 16  Boundaries and Coupling Relations
text:
16.0.1 Structural Definition of Coupling
System architecture is not determined only by the components that exist within a system, but by how tightly those components are connected. The strength and nature of these connections determine how easily a system can evolve, scale, and tolerate failure.
Coupling is therefore one of the most important structural properties of an architecture. However, in many architectural discussions coupling is treated as a subjective concept—described informally as “tight” or “loose” without precise structural criteria.
Within the ontology framework, coupling must be defined structurally rather than intuitively. Coupling emerges from specific relations between entities and can therefore be represented and analyzed explicitly.
Coupling represents the degree of dependency between architectural entities.
Two entities are coupled when the behavior, availability, or structure of one entity directly affects another. In ontology terms, coupling arises from relations such as:
The nature of these relations determines the type and strength of coupling.
For example:
By representing these relations explicitly, the ontology allows coupling to be analyzed as a property of the architectural graph rather than as an informal judgment.

title: 16  Boundaries and Coupling Relations
text:
16.1 Coupling Examples by Type

16.1.1 Synchronous Coupling Example
Tight Synchronous Coupling:
  Frontend Service → API Service → Database
  
Characteristics:
  - Frontend waits for API response
  - API waits for Database query
  - Total latency = sum of all latencies
  - Failure at any point breaks entire chain
  
Problems:
  - Cascading failures
  - Poor performance under load
  - Difficult to scale independently
  
When to use:
  - Request-response patterns where immediate response needed
  - Simple, small-scale systems
  - Strong consistency requirements


16.1.2 Asynchronous Coupling Example
Loose Asynchronous Coupling:
  Order Service → Message Queue → Inventory Service
                              → Email Service
                              → Analytics Service
  
Characteristics:
  - Order Service publishes event and continues
  - Consumers process independently
  - Failure of one consumer doesn't affect others
  - Each service scales independently
  
Benefits:
  - Improved resilience
  - Better scalability
  - Looser coupling
  
When to use:
  - Event-driven workflows
  - High-throughput systems
  - Loose coupling needed


16.1.3 Data Coupling Example
Data Coupling:
  Order Service reads Product Data
  Order Service reads User Data
  Order Service writes Order Data
  
Characteristics:
  - Shared data creates dependency
  - Changes to data structure affect all readers
  - Data ownership unclear
  
Implications:
  - Need for data versioning
  - Schema changes require coordination
  - Data consistency challenges


16.1.4 Control Coupling Example
Control Coupling:
  Orchestrator Service invokes Worker Service A
  Orchestrator Service invokes Worker Service B
  Orchestrator Service invokes Worker Service C
  
Characteristics:
  - Orchestrator controls execution flow
  - Workers depend on orchestrator
  - Central coordination point
  
Implications:
  - Orchestrator becomes bottleneck
  - Workers can't operate independently
  - Complex orchestration logic

title: 16  Boundaries and Coupling Relations
text:
16.2 Boundary Definition Examples

16.2.1 Well-Defined Boundary
Payment Service (Well-Defined Boundary)

Interface:
  POST /api/payments/process
  Request: PaymentRequest
  Response: PaymentResponse
  
Internal Implementation:
  - Payment validation logic
  - Fraud detection
  - Payment gateway integration
  - Transaction persistence
  
Boundary Characteristics:
  - Clear API contract
  - Internal details hidden
  - Can be replaced without affecting callers
  - Can be scaled independently
  - Can be tested in isolation
  
Benefits:
  - Easy to understand
  - Easy to maintain
  - Easy to evolve
  - Easy to test


16.2.2 Poorly Defined Boundary
Monolithic Order Processing (Poorly Defined Boundary)

Mixed Responsibilities:
  - Order validation
  - Payment processing
  - Inventory management
  - Email notifications
  - User authentication
  - Product catalog queries
  
Boundary Problems:
  - Multiple responsibilities mixed together
  - Difficult to separate concerns
  - Changes to one area affect others
  - Hard to test in isolation
  - Hard to scale independently
  
Consequences:
  - High coupling
  - Low cohesion
  - Difficult maintenance
  - Slow development
  - Fragile system

title: 16  Boundaries and Coupling Relations
text:
16.3 Interface Boundary Examples

16.3.1 API Interface Boundary
API Gateway Interface (External Boundary)

Purpose: External access to system services

Characteristics:
  - HTTP/HTTPS protocol
  - RESTful design
  - Authentication required
  - Rate limiting applied
  - Input validation

Benefits:
  - Single entry point
  - Consistent security
  - Controlled access
  - Monitoring and logging
  - API version management

Components Behind Interface:
  - Multiple internal services
  - Load balancer
  - Authentication service
  - Rate limiting service


16.3.2 Service Interface Boundary
Payment Service Interface (Internal Boundary)

Purpose: Service-to-service communication

Characteristics:
  - Internal protocol (gRPC, internal HTTP)
  - Service authentication (mTLS)
  - High performance
  - Service discovery
  - Circuit breaker patterns

Benefits:
  - Efficient communication
  - Secure internal traffic
  - Service isolation
  - Independent deployment
  - Technology diversity


16.3.3 Event Interface Boundary
Event Stream Interface (Asynchronous Boundary)

Purpose: Event-driven communication

Characteristics:
  - Publish-subscribe pattern
  - Message broker
  - Event schema definitions
  - Delivery guarantees
  - Consumer groups

Benefits:
  - Loose coupling
  - Temporal decoupling
  - Scalability
  - Resilience
  - Flexibility

title: 16  Boundaries and Coupling Relations
text:
16.4 Coupling Reduction Strategies

16.4.1 Strategy 1: Introduce Message Queue
Before (Tight Coupling):
  Service A → Service B → Service C
  
  Problem: Failure in B blocks entire chain

After (Loose Coupling with Queue):
  Service A → Message Queue → Service B
                              → Service C
  
  Benefits:
    - Service A doesn't wait for B or C
    - B and C can operate independently
    - Queue buffers load
    - Failure isolation


16.4.2 Strategy 2: Use API Gateway
Before (Multiple Direct Dependencies):
  Client → Service A
  Client → Service B
  Client → Service C
  
  Problem: Client knows about all services

After (API Gateway Pattern):
  Client → API Gateway → Service A
                    → Service B
                    → Service C
  
  Benefits:
    - Single entry point
    - Service discovery
    - Load balancing
    - Security enforcement
    - Protocol translation


16.4.3 Strategy 3: Implement Circuit Breaker
Before (Cascading Failures):
  Service A calls Service B
  Service B fails
  Service A fails
  Client fails

After (Circuit Breaker Pattern):
  Service A calls Service B (with circuit breaker)
  Service B fails
  Circuit breaker opens
  Service A returns fallback response
  System continues operating

Benefits:
    - Failure isolation
    - Fallback behavior
    - System resilience
    - Graceful degradation


16.4.4 Strategy 4: Event Sourcing
Before (Shared Database Coupling):
  Service A and Service B both write to Database
  Database schema becomes coupling point
  Changes affect both services

After (Event Sourcing):
  Service A emits events
  Service B emits events
  Event store persists events
  Each service rebuilds state from events

Benefits:
    - Decoupled data access
    - Audit trail
    - Event replay
    - Temporal queries



16.4.5 Directionality and Visualization of Relations
Relations between entities are typically directional.
Directionality indicates the direction of dependency or interaction between architectural elements. For example:

if component A calls component B, the relation is directed from A to B
if component A depends on component B, the dependency flows from A toward B

Representing direction explicitly is essential for analyzing execution paths, dependency chains, and failure propagation.
When visualizing architectural graphs, several conventions help maintain clarity.
First, directional relations are typically represented using arrows that indicate dependency or invocation flow.
Second, containment relations are often represented through hierarchical structures rather than arrows.
Third, different relation types may be distinguished using visual styles such as line types or colors, allowing invocation paths, data flows, and event streams to be visually separated.
These visualization conventions allow the ontology graph to function not only as a formal representation of architecture but also as a clear visual model of system structure and interaction.

title: 17  Interaction Models as Relation Patterns
text:
17.0.1 Request–Response
Relations describe individual connections between entities, but real system behavior emerges from recurring structures of relations rather than isolated links. When certain relation configurations appear repeatedly across systems, they form recognizable interaction models.
An interaction model is therefore a pattern of relations that defines how components coordinate behavior, exchange information, and produce system outcomes. These models capture the operational structure of a system beyond simple dependency graphs.
Within the ontology, interaction models are not treated as separate entity types. Instead, they are understood as relation patterns that can be recognized within the architectural graph.
The request–response model represents the most common interaction pattern in software systems.
In this model, one component sends a request to another component through a defined interface. The receiving component processes the request and returns a response.
The interaction structure typically involves the following relations:
This model is usually associated with synchronous communication mechanisms such as HTTP APIs, RPC calls, or internal service invocations.
Request–response interactions create strong temporal coupling, because the requesting component must wait for the responding component to complete its operation.
Despite this coupling, the model remains widely used because it provides clear control flow and predictable response semantics.

title: 17  Interaction Models as Relation Patterns
text:
17.1 Interaction Model Examples

17.1.1 Request-Response Example
Example: User Profile Lookup

Components:
  - Web Frontend (client)
  - User Service (server)
  - Database (storage)

Interaction Flow:
  1. Frontend calls User Service
     Request: GET /api/users/{id}
  
  2. User Service implements interface
     Receives request
     Validates user ID
     Queries database
  
  3. User Service reads from Database
     Query: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?
  
  4. Database returns user data
     Response: { id, name, email, ... }
  
  5. User Service returns response to Frontend
     Response: { id, name, email, ... }

Characteristics:
  - Synchronous interaction
  - Client waits for response
  - Single request-response cycle
  - Temporal coupling between components

Use Cases:
  - API requests where immediate response needed
  - Simple queries and operations
  - Strong consistency required
  - Low-latency interactions

Benefits:
  - Simple to understand and implement
  - Predictable behavior
  - Clear error handling
  - Easy to debug

Challenges:
  - Cascading failures
  - Poor performance under load
  - Tight coupling between components
  - Difficult to scale independently


17.1.2 Event-Driven Example
Example: Order Processing Event Flow

Components:
  - Order Service (producer)
  - Inventory Service (consumer)
  - Email Service (consumer)
  - Analytics Service (consumer)
  - Message Broker (coordination)

Interaction Flow:
  1. Order Service creates order
     Processes order locally
     Emits OrderCreated event
  
  2. Order Service emits event to Message Broker
     Event: { order_id, user_id, items, total, timestamp }
     Topic: orders.created
  
  3. Message Broker distributes event
     Publishes to all subscribers
     Ensures delivery
  
  4. Inventory Service consumes event
     Receives OrderCreated event
     Reserves inventory
     Updates stock levels
  
  5. Email Service consumes event
     Receives OrderCreated event
     Sends confirmation email
     Updates customer communication
  
  6. Analytics Service consumes event
     Receives OrderCreated event
     Updates analytics metrics
     Generates reports

Characteristics:
  - Asynchronous interaction
  - Producer doesn't know consumers
  - Multiple consumers possible
  - Temporal decoupling

Use Cases:
  - Notifications and alerts
  - Data synchronization
  - Loose coupling needed
  - High-throughput systems

Benefits:
  - Loose coupling
  - Scalability
  - Resilience
  - Flexibility

Challenges:
  - Eventual consistency
  - Complex debugging
  - Event ordering challenges
  - Consumer failure handling


17.1.3 Pipeline Example
Example: Data Processing Pipeline

Components:
  - Ingestion Worker (stage 1)
  - Transformation Engine (stage 2)
  - Validation Engine (stage 3)
  - Storage Component (stage 4)

Interaction Flow:
  1. Ingestion Worker reads raw data
     Input: Raw data files
     Output: Structured records
  
  2. Ingestion Worker writes to Transformation Engine
     Passes structured records
     Triggers next stage
  
  3. Transformation Engine processes data
     Applies business rules
     Normalizes formats
     Enriches data
  
  4. Transformation Engine writes to Validation Engine
     Passes transformed data
     Triggers next stage
  
  5. Validation Engine validates data
     Checks data quality
     Validates schemas
     Filters invalid records
  
  6. Validation Engine writes to Storage
     Passes validated data
     Completes pipeline

Characteristics:
  - Sequential data flow
  - Each stage processes in order
  - Data transformation focus
  - Linear progression

Use Cases:
  - Data ETL processes
  - Analytics pipelines
  - Machine learning workflows
  - Content processing

Benefits:
  - Clear data flow
  - Modular stages
  - Easy to add/remove stages
  - Process visibility

Challenges:
  - Sequential bottlenecks
  - Error handling complexity
  - Backpressure management
  - Data format compatibility


17.1.4 Orchestration Example
Example: Order Fulfillment Orchestration

Components:
  - Orchestrator Service (central controller)
  - Payment Service (payment processing)
  - Inventory Service (stock management)
  - Shipping Service (fulfillment)
  - Notification Service (communication)

Interaction Flow:
  1. Orchestrator receives order
     Starts orchestration workflow
  
  2. Orchestrator invokes Payment Service
     Command: Process payment for order
     Waits for completion
  
  3. Payment Service processes payment
     Charges payment method
     Returns success/failure
  
  4. Orchestrator invokes Inventory Service
     Command: Reserve items for order
     Waits for completion
  
  5. Inventory Service reserves inventory
     Checks stock availability
     Updates inventory levels
     Returns success/failure
  
  6. Orchestrator invokes Shipping Service
     Command: Create shipment for order
     Waits for completion
  
  7. Shipping Service creates shipment
     Generates shipping label
     Schedules pickup
     Returns tracking number
  
  8. Orchestrator invokes Notification Service
     Command: Send order confirmation
     Waits for completion
  
  9. Notification Service sends notification
     Emails customer
     SMS customer
     Returns success/failure
  
  10. Orchestrator completes workflow
      Marks order as fulfilled
      Returns final status

Characteristics:
  - Centralized control
  - Explicit workflow
  - Sequential execution
  - Strong coordination

Use Cases:
  - Complex business processes
  - Multi-step workflows
  - Transactional operations
  - Process automation

Benefits:
  - Centralized control
  - Clear workflow visibility
  - Easy error handling
  - Transaction management

Challenges:
  - Orchestrator bottleneck
  - Single point of failure
  - Complexity in orchestrator
  - Tight coupling to orchestrator


17.1.5 Choreography Example
Example: Order Processing Choreography

Components:
  - Order Service (initiator)
  - Inventory Service (participant)
  - Payment Service (participant)
  - Shipping Service (participant)
  - Notification Service (participant)
  - Event Broker (coordination)

Interaction Flow:
  1. Order Service creates order
     Emits OrderCreated event
  
  2. Inventory Service consumes OrderCreated
     Receives event
     Reserves inventory
     Emits InventoryReserved event
     Or emits InventoryUnavailable event if stock insufficient
  
  3. Payment Service consumes InventoryReserved
     Receives event
     Processes payment
     Emits PaymentCompleted event
     Or emits PaymentFailed event if payment declined
  
  4. Shipping Service consumes PaymentCompleted
     Receives event
     Creates shipment
     Emits OrderShipped event
  
  5. Notification Service consumes OrderShipped
     Receives event
     Sends notification
     Emits NotificationSent event
  
  6. Order Service consumes final events
     Updates order status
     Completes workflow

Characteristics:
  - Decentralized control
  - Event-driven coordination
  - Independent components
  - Loose coupling

Use Cases:
  - Event-driven architectures
  - High-scale systems
  - Loose coupling required
  - Independent evolution

Benefits:
  - Loose coupling
  - Independent scaling
  - Fault isolation
  - Flexibility

Challenges:
  - Complex event flows
  - Difficult debugging
  - Event ordering issues
  - No central coordinator


17.1.6 Agentic Tool-Calling Example
Example: Task Execution Agent

Components:
  - Agent Controller (reasoning engine)
  - LLM Engine (decision making)
  - Tool Executor (tool invocation)
  - Tool A (database query)
  - Tool B (web search)
  - Tool C (file operation)
  - Memory Store (context management)

Interaction Flow:
  1. User provides task
     Request: "Find recent sales data and analyze trends"
  
  2. Agent Controller calls LLM Engine
     Input: Task description
     Request: Generate execution plan
  
  3. LLM Engine generates plan
     Output: Multi-step plan
     Steps: Query database, Analyze data, Generate report
  
  4. Agent Controller executes Step 1
     Invokes Tool Executor with Tool A
     Command: Query sales data from last 30 days
  
  5. Tool Executor invokes Tool A
     Executes database query
     Returns sales data
  
  6. Agent Controller receives result
     Stores in Memory Store
     Proceeds to Step 2
  
  7. Agent Controller executes Step 2
     Calls LLM Engine with data
     Request: Analyze trends in sales data
  
  8. LLM Engine analyzes data
     Identifies trends
     Returns analysis results
  
  9. Agent Controller executes Step 3
     Invokes Tool Executor with Tool C
     Command: Save analysis report to file
  
  10. Tool Executor invokes Tool C
      Writes report to file
      Returns confirmation
  
  11. Agent Controller completes task
      Synthesizes results
      Returns final response to user

Characteristics:
  - Dynamic decision making
  - Runtime tool selection
  - Iterative reasoning
  - Adaptive execution

Use Cases:
  - AI-powered automation
  - Complex task execution
  - Dynamic workflows
  - Intelligent assistants

Benefits:
  - Flexibility
  - Adaptability
  - Intelligence
  - Automation

Challenges:
  - Unpredictable behavior
  - Tool failure handling
  - Reasoning complexity
  - Performance variability

title: 17  Interaction Models as Relation Patterns
text:
17.2 Interaction Model Comparison

17.2.1 Temporal Coupling Comparison
Request-Response:
  Coupling: High (synchronous)
  Latency: High (sum of all latencies)
  Resilience: Low (cascading failures)
  Scalability: Low (tight coupling)

Event-Driven:
  Coupling: Low (asynchronous)
  Latency: Low (no waiting)
  Resilience: High (isolated failures)
  Scalability: High (independent scaling)

Pipeline:
  Coupling: Medium (sequential)
  Latency: Medium (stages add latency)
  Resilience: Medium (stage failures)
  Scalability: Medium (stage independence)

Orchestration:
  Coupling: High (centralized)
  Latency: High (sequential steps)
  Resilience: Low (orchestrator dependency)
  Scalability: Low (orchestrator bottleneck)

Choreography:
  Coupling: Low (event-based)
  Latency: Low (asynchronous)
  Resilience: High (isolated failures)
  Scalability: High (independent scaling)

Agentic:
  Coupling: Variable (dynamic)
  Latency: Variable (iterative)
  Resilience: Medium (depends on tools)
  Scalability: Medium (depends on reasoning)


17.2.2 Use Case Recommendations
Choose Request-Response when:
  - Immediate response required
  - Simple interactions
  - Strong consistency needed
  - Low latency acceptable

Choose Event-Driven when:
  - Loose coupling needed
  - Multiple consumers
  - High throughput required
  - Eventual consistency acceptable

Choose Pipeline when:
  - Data transformation focus
  - Sequential processing
  - Clear stages needed
  - Data flow visibility important

Choose Orchestration when:
  - Complex workflows
  - Central control needed
  - Transaction semantics required
  - Process visibility important

Choose Choreography when:
  - Independent components
  - Loose coupling preferred
  - High scalability needed
  - Independent evolution desired

Choose Agentic when:
  - Dynamic decision making
  - Complex, unstructured tasks
  - AI-powered automation
  - Adaptive execution needed



17.2.3 Event-Driven
The event-driven interaction model is based on asynchronous message propagation.
In this pattern, components emit events describing state changes or completed operations. Other components may subscribe to these events and react when they occur.
The relation structure typically includes:

a component emits an event
an event channel distributes the event
one or more components consume the event

Unlike request–response interactions, event-driven systems do not require producers to know which components will consume the event.
This model introduces temporal decoupling, allowing producers and consumers to operate independently. It is commonly used in distributed systems that require scalability and resilience.
Event-driven architectures often rely on message brokers, event streams, or publish–subscribe infrastructures.


17.2.4 Pipeline and Stream
The pipeline interaction model represents systems in which data flows through a sequence of processing stages.
In this structure, each component performs a transformation on incoming data and passes the result to the next stage of the pipeline.
The relation structure typically includes:

components that read input data
components that write transformed output
sequential data flows connecting stages

Pipelines are common in batch processing systems, data analytics workflows, and machine learning pipelines.
A closely related structure is the stream processing model, where data flows continuously rather than in discrete batches.
Both pipeline and stream architectures emphasize data flow as the primary organizing principle of the system.


17.2.5 Orchestration vs Choreography
Complex systems often involve multiple interacting components that must coordinate their behavior.
Two major coordination models exist.
Orchestration
In orchestration, a central component explicitly controls the execution of other components. The orchestrator determines the order of operations and directs tasks through explicit invocation relations.
The relation structure often includes:

an orchestration component that invokes multiple tasks
workflow definitions describing execution order
centralized control over execution logic

Orchestration provides strong control over process flow but may introduce central coordination dependencies.
Choreography
In choreography, coordination emerges from event interactions between components rather than from a central controller.
Each component reacts to events emitted by others and performs its own operations accordingly.
The relation structure includes:

components that emit events
other components that consume those events
decentralized control logic distributed across the system

Choreography reduces centralized dependencies and allows more flexible system evolution.


17.2.6 Agentic Tool-Calling
Recent architectures based on language models and autonomous agents introduce a new interaction model often described as tool-calling.
In this model, an agent component dynamically selects and invokes tools in order to accomplish a task.
The interaction structure typically includes:

an agent component that interprets goals or prompts
tool interfaces representing available operations
invocation relations between the agent and selected tools
feedback loops where tool outputs influence subsequent decisions

Unlike traditional workflow orchestration, tool-calling interactions are often dynamic and decision-driven. The agent determines which tools to invoke based on runtime reasoning rather than predetermined execution sequences.
From an ontology perspective, agentic tool-calling can be represented as a pattern combining:

invocation relations (calls)
workflow coordination
dynamic decision logic

This interaction model is increasingly relevant in systems that integrate AI agents, automated planning systems, and adaptive workflows.

By representing interaction models as relation patterns rather than fixed constructs, the ontology allows architectural structures to be described flexibly while still capturing the recurring coordination patterns that shape system behavior.

title: 18  System Type Taxonomy (v0.1)
text:
18.0.1 Why System Types Must Be Finite and Stable
Architectural representations benefit from a stable classification of system types. While individual systems vary widely in implementation, many share recognizable structural patterns. A taxonomy of system types enables architectural descriptions to be compared, indexed, and analyzed across large collections of systems.
Within the ontology, system types provide a high-level categorization of architectural structures. They describe the dominant operational model of a system rather than its specific implementation details.
The taxonomy defined in Ontology v0.1 focuses on a small set of system categories that appear consistently across software ecosystems.
A system type taxonomy must remain limited and stable.
If the number of types grows without constraint, classification becomes inconsistent. Different architects may assign different type labels to similar systems, preventing meaningful comparison across blueprint datasets.
A small and stable set of system types ensures that:
System types therefore function as structural anchors rather than descriptive labels. Each type represents a recurring architectural organization that appears across many systems.
Because architectural styles evolve slowly compared to implementation technologies, the number of system types should remain relatively constant across ontology versions.

title: 19  Component Type Taxonomy (v0.1)
text:
While system types classify entire architectures, component types classify the structural elements that compose those systems. A stable taxonomy of component types enables architectural descriptions to remain consistent across domains, technologies, and implementation environments.
Component types describe the functional role of a component within the architecture, rather than its implementation details. For example, a database component may be implemented using many different technologies, but its architectural role as a storage component remains constant.
The component taxonomy defined in Ontology v0.1 focuses on a small set of structural roles that appear across most software systems. These roles capture the primary responsibilities that components perform within system architectures.

19.0.1 Frontend and Interface Components
Frontend and interface components represent the points of interaction between the system and external actors. These actors may be human users, external systems, or automated processes.
Frontend components provide user-facing interaction mechanisms. Examples include graphical web interfaces, desktop interfaces, and mobile interfaces. These components focus on presenting information and collecting user input.
Interface components provide programmatic access to system capabilities. These interfaces often appear as APIs, command-line interfaces, or event endpoints.
The architectural role of these components is to expose system capabilities while maintaining a controlled boundary between internal components and external actors.
Frontend Examples:
React Web Application:
  - Provides browser-based user interface
  - Manages client-side state
  - Communicates with backend APIs
  
Mobile Application:
  - Provides mobile user interface
  - Accesses device capabilities
  - Offline functionality support
  
Desktop Application:
  - Provides desktop user interface
  - Integrates with operating system
  - Native performance

CLI Tool:
  - Provides command-line interface
  - Accepts command-line arguments
  - Returns structured output
Interface Examples:
REST API:
  - HTTP/HTTPS protocol
  - JSON/XML data format
  - Standard HTTP methods
  
GraphQL API:
  - Single endpoint
  - Query language for data
  - Flexible data retrieval
  
gRPC API:
  - Protocol Buffers
  - High-performance RPC
  - Streaming support
  
Event Stream:
  - Publish-subscribe model
  - Real-time events
  - Multiple consumers
  
Command Interface:
  - Programmatic commands
  - Scriptable interface
  - Batch processing support


19.0.2 Compute Components
Compute components perform the core processing logic of the system. They implement the computational behavior required to fulfill system capabilities.
Several structural roles commonly appear within this category.
Service components process incoming requests and apply business logic. They often expose APIs and coordinate interactions with other components.
Worker components execute background processing tasks such as data transformations, asynchronous jobs, or long-running computations.
Engine components implement specialized execution logic. Examples include workflow engines, rule engines, recommendation engines, or model inference engines.
Compute components therefore represent the active processing layer of the system architecture.
Service Examples:
API Service:
  - Handles HTTP requests
  - Implements business logic
  - Coordinates with other services
  
Business Logic Service:
  - Implements domain rules
  - Processes business operations
  - Maintains domain state
  
Integration Service:
  - Integrates with external systems
  - Handles data transformation
  - Manages external API calls
Worker Examples:
Background Job Worker:
  - Processes scheduled jobs
  - Executes long-running tasks
  - Handles batch operations
  
Data Processing Worker:
  - Transforms data
  - Applies business rules
  - Generates reports
  
Notification Worker:
  - Sends notifications
  - Handles email/SMS
  - Manages delivery retries
Engine Examples:
Workflow Engine:
  - Orchestrates workflows
  - Manages task execution
  - Handles retries and errors
  
Rule Engine:
  - Evaluates business rules
  - Makes decisions
  - Applies policies
  
ML Inference Engine:
  - Runs machine learning models
  - Makes predictions
  - Processes inference requests
  
Search Engine:
  - Executes searches
  - Ranks results
  - Handles queries


19.0.3 Storage Components
Storage components manage the persistence and retrieval of system data.
These components maintain data across system operations and ensure that information remains available beyond the execution of individual tasks.
Typical storage components include:

relational or document databases
distributed key–value stores
caching systems
vector databases used for embedding storage and similarity search

Storage components are often associated with specific data entities within the ontology. They define where system data resides and how it is accessed.
Because storage components manage durable state, they often represent critical architectural dependencies.
Storage Examples:
Relational Database:
  - Structured data storage
  - ACID transactions
  - SQL queries
  - Examples: PostgreSQL, MySQL
  
Document Database:
  - Flexible schema
  - JSON documents
  - Nested data structures
  - Examples: MongoDB, CouchDB
  
Key-Value Store:
  - High-performance access
  - Simple data model
  - Low latency
  - Examples: Redis, DynamoDB
  
Object Storage:
  - Large file storage
  - Scalable
  - Cost-effective
  - Examples: S3, Azure Blob
  
Vector Database:
  - Embedding storage
  - Similarity search
  - ML applications
  - Examples: Pinecone, Weaviate
Cache Examples:
In-Memory Cache:
  - Fast access
  - Volatile storage
  - Session data
  - Examples: Redis, Memcached
  
CDN Cache:
  - Content delivery
  - Geographic distribution
  - Static assets
  - Examples: Cloudflare, Akamai
  
Application Cache:
  - Response caching
  - Computed results
  - Performance optimization
  - Examples: Built-in caches


19.0.4 Coordination Components
Coordination components manage the temporal and structural coordination of system activities.
These components regulate how tasks are scheduled, how components communicate asynchronously, and how workflows are executed.
Common coordination roles include:
Queue components buffer tasks or messages between producers and consumers. They decouple components and allow asynchronous communication.
Scheduler components initiate tasks according to time-based or conditional triggers.
Orchestrator components manage multi-step workflows and coordinate execution across multiple services or tasks.
Coordination components are particularly important in distributed systems, where many components must interact without direct synchronous dependencies.
Queue Examples:
Message Queue:
  - Message buffering
  - FIFO ordering
  - At-least-once delivery
  - Examples: RabbitMQ, SQS
  
Task Queue:
  - Job scheduling
  - Worker coordination
  - Priority support
  - Examples: Celery, Sidekiq
  
Event Queue:
  - Event streaming
  - Publish-subscribe
  - Multiple consumers
  - Examples: Kafka, Pulsar
Scheduler Examples:
Cron Scheduler:
  - Time-based triggers
  - Recurring jobs
  - Cron expressions
  - Examples: Quartz, Sidekiq-Scheduler
  
Event Scheduler:
  - Event-based triggers
  - Conditional execution
  - Complex schedules
  - Examples: Temporal, Cadence
  
Resource Scheduler:
  - Resource allocation
  - Load balancing
  - Priority scheduling
  - Examples: Kubernetes Scheduler
Orchestrator Examples:
Workflow Orchestrator:
  - Workflow coordination
  - Step execution
  - Error handling
  - Examples: Airflow, Temporal
  
Service Orchestrator:
  - Service coordination
  - Dependency management
  - Service discovery
  - Examples: Kubernetes, Nomad
  
Process Orchestrator:
  - Process management
  - Lifecycle control
  - Scaling operations
  - Examples: Docker Swarm, ECS


19.0.5 Observability Components
Observability components provide visibility into the behavior and performance of the system.
These components collect and analyze operational information, allowing engineers to understand system behavior, detect failures, and diagnose performance issues.
Typical observability roles include:
Log systems that record operational events and system messages.
Metrics systems that collect quantitative measurements such as request latency, throughput, and resource usage.
Tracing systems that record the execution path of requests as they propagate across components.
Observability components do not directly implement business functionality, but they play a critical role in maintaining system reliability and operational transparency.
Logging Examples:
Application Logger:
  - Application events
  - Structured logs
  - Log levels (debug, info, warn, error)
  - Examples: Log4j, Winston
  
Access Logger:
  - HTTP access logs
  - Request tracking
  - Security auditing
  - Examples: Nginx logs, Apache logs
  
Audit Logger:
  - Compliance logging
  - Security events
  - Immutable records
  - Examples: CloudTrail, Audit Logs
Metrics Examples:
Application Metrics:
  - Request rate
  - Response time
  - Error rate
  - Examples: Prometheus, StatsD
  
System Metrics:
  - CPU usage
  - Memory usage
  - Disk I/O
  - Examples: Node Exporter, Collectd
  
Business Metrics:
  - Order count
  - Revenue
  - User engagement
  - Examples: Custom metrics, Datadog
Tracing Examples:
Distributed Tracing:
  - Request tracing
  - Service dependencies
  - Performance analysis
  - Examples: Jaeger, Zipkin, OpenTelemetry
  
Transaction Tracing:
  - Database queries
  - External API calls
  - Transaction performance
  - Examples: APM tools, New Relic
  
User Journey Tracing:
  - User interactions
  - Session tracking
  - UX analysis
  - Examples: Session replay tools


Together, these component types form a minimal taxonomy capable of describing the primary structural roles present in most system architectures.
By categorizing components according to their architectural function, the ontology enables blueprint representations to remain consistent across different technologies while preserving the essential structural characteristics of the system.

title: 20  Architecture Style Taxonomy (v0.1)
text:
While system types classify what kind of system exists, architectural styles describe how the internal structure of that system is organized. An architecture style represents a recurring structural arrangement of components, interfaces, and interaction patterns.
Architectural styles capture higher-level design strategies that shape the organization of software systems. These strategies influence how responsibilities are distributed, how components interact, and how systems evolve over time.
Within the ontology, architecture styles function as structural descriptors that characterize the dominant organization pattern of a system.

20.0.1 Layered Architecture
Layered architecture organizes components into hierarchical layers, where each layer performs a specific responsibility and interacts primarily with adjacent layers.
Typical layers include:

presentation or interface layer
application or service layer
domain logic layer
data persistence layer

In layered systems, dependencies typically flow in one direction—from higher layers toward lower layers. This structure promotes separation of concerns and simplifies reasoning about system organization.
Layered architectures are commonly found in enterprise applications, web services, and traditional backend systems.
Example: E-commerce Layered Architecture
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Presentation Layer                     │
│  (Web UI, Mobile App)                   │
└────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
             │ HTTP calls
┌────────────▼────────────────────────────┐
│  Application Layer                       │
│  (Order Service, User Service)           │
└────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
             │ Business logic
┌────────────▼────────────────────────────┐
│  Domain Layer                           │
│  (Order Domain, User Domain)            │
└────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
             │ Domain models
┌────────────▼────────────────────────────┐
│  Data Layer                             │
│  (Database, Cache, File Storage)       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Benefits:
  - Clear separation of concerns
  - Easy to understand
  - Testable layers
  - Reusable components

Challenges:
  - Can become rigid
  - Performance overhead
  - Changes ripple across layers
  - May not fit all systems


20.0.2 Modular Monolith
A modular monolith is a system that runs as a single deployable unit while maintaining strong internal modular boundaries.
In this architecture style, components are organized into modules that encapsulate distinct responsibilities. These modules interact through well-defined interfaces but are packaged and deployed as a single application.
The modular monolith balances two objectives:

strong internal structure and separation of responsibilities
operational simplicity through single-unit deployment

This style is often used in systems that require clear modularity but do not yet require distributed deployment.
Example: Modular Monolith E-commerce System
Single Application:
  ├── Module: User Management
  │   ├── User API
  │   ├── User Logic
  │   └── User Storage
  │
  ├── Module: Order Processing
  │   ├── Order API
  │   ├── Order Logic
  │   └── Order Storage
  │
  ├── Module: Payment Processing
  │   ├── Payment API
  │   ├── Payment Logic
  │   └── Payment Storage
  │
  └── Module: Inventory Management
      ├── Inventory API
      ├── Inventory Logic
      └── Inventory Storage

Benefits:
  - Simpler deployment
  - Easier testing
  - Clear module boundaries
  - Good starting point

Challenges:
  - Scaling limitations
  - Single point of failure
  - Module independence
  - Technology constraints

When to use:
  - Small to medium teams
  - Simple deployment needs
  - Rapid development
  - Monolithic simplicity needed


20.0.3 Microservices
Microservice architectures decompose systems into independently deployable services that communicate through network interfaces.
Each service typically encapsulates a specific capability and maintains control over its own data and runtime environment.
Key characteristics of microservice architectures include:

service-level deployment boundaries
network-based communication between components
independent scaling of services
decentralized data ownership

Microservice architectures increase system flexibility and scalability but introduce additional operational complexity.
Example: E-commerce Microservices
Service A: User Service
  - Manages user accounts
  - Exposes user API
  - Owns user database

Service B: Order Service
  - Processes orders
  - Exposes order API
  - Owns order database

Service C: Inventory Service
  - Manages inventory
  - Exposes inventory API
  - Owns inventory database

Service D: Payment Service
  - Processes payments
  - Exposes payment API
  - Owns transaction database

Communication:
  - HTTP/gRPC APIs
  - Event-driven messaging
  - Service discovery
  - API gateway routing

Benefits:
  - Independent scaling
  - Technology diversity
  - Fault isolation
  - Team autonomy

Challenges:
  - Operational complexity
  - Distributed systems challenges
  - Network overhead
  - Data consistency

When to use:
  - Large systems
  - Multiple teams
  - Independent scaling needs
  - Technology diversity


20.0.4 Event-Driven Architecture
Event-driven architectures organize system behavior around asynchronous event propagation.
In this style, components emit events that describe state changes or completed operations. Other components react to these events without requiring direct invocation relationships.
Event-driven systems often include components such as event producers, message brokers, and event consumers.
This architectural style enables temporal decoupling between components and supports high scalability in distributed environments.
Example: Event-Driven Order System
Event Producers:
  - Order Service emits: OrderCreated, OrderCancelled
  - Payment Service emits: PaymentCompleted, PaymentFailed
  - Shipping Service emits: OrderShipped, OrderDelivered

Message Broker:
  - Kafka topic: orders
  - Kafka topic: payments
  - Kafka topic: shipments

Event Consumers:
  - Inventory Service consumes OrderCreated
  - Email Service consumes OrderCreated, OrderShipped
  - Analytics Service consumes all events
  - Notification Service consumes OrderDelivered

Benefits:
  - Loose coupling
  - Temporal decoupling
  - Scalability
  - Flexibility

Challenges:
  - Eventual consistency
  - Debugging complexity
  - Event ordering
  - Consumer failure handling

When to use:
  - High throughput needed
  - Loose coupling desired
  - Multiple consumers
  - Async processing needed


20.0.5 Pipeline Architecture
Pipeline architectures organize computation as a sequence of processing stages through which data flows.
Each stage performs a transformation on the incoming data before passing it to the next stage. Pipelines may operate on batch datasets or continuous data streams.
This style is commonly used in:

data processing systems
analytics pipelines
machine learning workflows
media processing systems

Pipeline architectures emphasize data flow as the organizing principle of the system.
Example: Data Analytics Pipeline
Stage 1: Ingestion
  - Collects data from sources
  - Validates data format
  - Writes to staging area

Stage 2: Transformation
  - Cleans data
  - Applies business rules
  - Enriches data

Stage 3: Aggregation
  - Aggregates metrics
  - Computes summaries
  - Generates insights

Stage 4: Storage
  - Writes to warehouse
  - Updates indexes
  - Creates reports

Data Flow:
  Source → Ingestion → Transformation → Aggregation → Storage

Benefits:
  - Clear data flow
  - Modular stages
  - Easy to monitor
  - Scalable stages

Challenges:
  - Sequential bottlenecks
  - Error handling
  - Backpressure
  - Stage compatibility

When to use:
  - Data processing
  - Analytics workflows
  - ETL processes
  - ML pipelines


20.0.6 Plugin-Based Architecture
Plugin-based architectures support extensibility through dynamically loadable components.
The core system defines extension points that allow external modules or plugins to introduce additional functionality without modifying the core system.
This style is commonly found in:

development tools and editors
platform ecosystems
extensible frameworks

Plugin architectures enable flexible extension mechanisms and support ecosystem-driven development models.
Example: IDE Plugin System
Core IDE:
  - Editor component
  - Syntax highlighting
  - File management
  - UI framework

Extension Points:
  - Language support plugins
  - Build system plugins
  - Version control plugins
  - Code analysis plugins

Plugin Examples:
  - Python Language Plugin
  - Maven Build Plugin
  - Git Integration Plugin
  - Linting Plugin

Plugin Interface:
  - Plugin lifecycle (load, initialize, activate)
  - Extension point registration
  - Service provision
  - UI integration

Benefits:
  - Extensibility
  - Third-party ecosystem
  - Customization
  - Modularity

Challenges:
  - Plugin compatibility
  - Security concerns
  - Version management
  - Quality control

When to use:
  - Extensibility needed
  - Third-party developers
  - Platform products
  - Tool frameworks


20.0.7 Hybrid Architectures
In practice, many systems combine elements from multiple architectural styles.
A system may, for example, combine microservices with event-driven communication, or embed pipeline processing stages within a layered application structure.
These systems are referred to as hybrid architectures.
Hybrid architectures arise because architectural styles represent design patterns rather than strict constraints. Systems often adopt multiple patterns to address different operational requirements.
Recognizing hybrid architectures is therefore essential for accurate architectural representation.
Example: Hybrid E-commerce Platform
Primary Style: Microservices
  - Independent services for different domains
  - Network-based communication
  - Independent deployment

Secondary Style: Event-Driven
  - Services communicate via events
  - Asynchronous processing
  - Loose coupling between services

Tertiary Style: Layered (within services)
  - Each service has layered structure
  - Presentation, application, data layers
  - Internal modularity

Result: System combines multiple architectural styles to address different needs:
  - Microservices for independent scaling
  - Event-driven for loose coupling
  - Layered for internal structure



20.0.8 Identifying Architecture Styles
Architecture styles can often be inferred from structural signals present in code repositories, configuration files, and system entry points.
Several types of signals are particularly useful for this purpose.
Repository structure
The organization of directories and modules can indicate architectural style. For example, layered directory structures may indicate layered architectures, while service-based repository structures may suggest microservices.
Dependency patterns
The dependency graph between modules or packages may reveal architectural boundaries and interaction structures.
Entry points
The presence of multiple independent service entry points may indicate a microservice architecture, while a single primary entry point may indicate a monolithic system.
Messaging infrastructure
Configuration files referencing message brokers or event streams may indicate event-driven architectures.
These structural signals form the basis for automated architecture detection methods introduced in later volumes of the series, particularly in the context of Blueprint Extraction.
By identifying architectural styles through observable structural patterns, blueprint representations can classify and analyze large collections of systems with greater consistency and accuracy.

title: 21  Pattern Hooks: Making Ontology Pattern-Aware
text:
21.0.1 Patterns as Reusable Structural Fragments
Architectural patterns represent reusable structural solutions that appear repeatedly across software systems. While the ontology defines the fundamental entities and relations used to describe systems, patterns capture recurring arrangements of those entities and relations.
For the Blueprint Architecture framework to support pattern discovery, pattern reuse, and architecture intelligence, the ontology must be pattern-aware. This means that the ontology should not only represent system structures but also provide the structural anchors necessary for identifying and describing recurring architectural patterns.
Pattern hooks serve this role. They connect the ontology representation of systems with the pattern catalog introduced in later volumes of the series.
A pattern can be understood as a reusable fragment of system structure that solves a recurring architectural problem.
Patterns do not represent entire systems. Instead, they capture partial configurations of components, interfaces, workflows, and relations that appear repeatedly in many systems.
Examples include structures such as:
Patterns are therefore structural templates that can be embedded into larger system architectures.
Within the ontology, patterns are not treated as primitive entities. Instead, they are expressed as subgraphs of the ontology structure.
